html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. LLM: large language model

  • When a multi-agent design is worth its cost
  • The orchestrator-worker architecture and how to brief subagents
  • Decomposition techniques for complex problems
  • Production concerns: state, errors, tracing, deployment

2When Multi-Agent Pays Off

Running case

Lumen Advisory and the Due-Diligence Research Tool

  • A private-equity client wants market and regulatory research on 40 companies per week
  • One agent runs out of context and takes hours; parallel subagents can each cover a company and a lead agent merges the findings
Factor Multi-agent fits Single agent or workflow fits
Parallelism Independent branches (companies, sources) Strong dependencies between steps
Information size More than one context window Fits in one window
Value of result High: justifies many tokens Low or routine
Shared context Little needed between branches Heavy shared state (most coding)
  • Reported figures: agents use about 4x the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about 15x; a lead-plus-subagents design beat a single agent by about 90 percent on a research eval, and parallelization cut research time by up to 90 percent. Token usage explained most performance variance.
  • Worth it only when value, parallelism and context size justify the cost; otherwise a workflow is cheaper and simpler.
Exam tip

Multi-agent is justified by parallelizable, high-value work that exceeds one context window. Tasks with heavy shared context or many dependencies (for example most coding) are poor fits.

3Orchestrator-Worker Design

Element Practice
Lead agent Plans, decomposes, delegates, synthesizes; saves the plan to external memory so it survives context limits
Subagents Own isolated context; return summaries, not raw transcripts
Brief Give each subagent a clear objective, output format, tool guidance and task boundaries to avoid duplicated work
Effort scaling Put explicit rules in the prompt: simple lookup = one agent with a few tool calls; complex research = many subagents
Verification A separate step checks claims and attaches sources
Tools Distinct purposes with clear descriptions; poor descriptions send agents down wrong paths
  • Context isolation keeps verbose exploration out of the lead's window (Module 6).
  • Parallel tool calls inside agents cut time further.
  • Start with broad queries and then narrow; use thinking as a planning scratchpad.

4Decomposition

Decomposition splits a complex problem into smaller solvable parts.

Style How Example
By sequence Ordered steps Extract, validate, enrich, draft
By data partition Split the data and run branches in parallel One subagent per company or document batch
By role Specialists for skills Legal-reading agent, financial-metrics agent
By dependency Graph of tasks; run independent nodes in parallel Build a plan, run in topological order
Hierarchical Orchestrator decomposes at run time Unknown number of files to edit
  • Decompose until each part has a clear input, output and check.
  • Minimize coupling between parts (little shared state).
  • Define the interface between parts (schema for hand-offs).
  • Keep human checkpoints at risky joins.

5Production Concerns

Concern Practice
State and errors Errors compound: checkpoint and resume instead of restarting; retries; let agents adapt when a tool fails
Debugging Non-deterministic runs: trace every agent decision and tool call; monitor decision patterns
Deployment Agents are mid-process during releases: use gradual (rainbow) deployments that shift traffic between versions
Latency A lead that waits for each batch is a bottleneck; asynchronous designs add parallelism but also complexity
Cost control Effort rules, step and token budgets, model tiering (cheaper subagents)
Evaluation Start with about 20 queries; LLM judge with a rubric; judge outcomes, not fixed paths; add human testing
Security Per-agent least privilege; treat subagent output as untrusted data
Exam tip

For long-running agent systems the architect's answer includes checkpointing, tracing, staged deployment and step or token budgets.

Exam tip

Multi-agent systems multiply tokens (about 15x chat): ask whether the value and parallelism justify the cost before choosing one.

6Exam Q&A

S1A research product must cover 40 independent companies per week, each needing many sources. Which design is most appropriate?

  • AOne agent that processes the 40 companies sequentially in a single conversation
  • BA single prompt containing all 40 companies and all source documents
  • CAn orchestrator-worker design with parallel subagents, each with its own context, and a lead that merges results
  • DA routing workflow that sends each company to a fixed three-step chain
Show the answer

Answer: C. Independent, high-value, context-heavy branches suit parallel subagents with isolated contexts and a lead that merges the findings.

S2Which task is the poorest fit for a multi-agent design?

  • AEditing tightly coupled code across files where every change depends on shared context
  • BResearching a broad topic across separate branches before merging the findings into one report
  • CReviewing a large set of independent contracts in parallel
  • DGathering information from many independent sources for a market report
Show the answer

Answer: A. Shared context and many dependencies make parallel agents inefficient.

S3What should a lead agent do so that the plan survives when the context fills?

  • AIncrease the temperature so that the plan is regenerated each time
  • BRepeat the plan in every subagent message to keep it visible
  • CAsk the user to re-enter the plan whenever the context grows
  • DSave the plan to external memory and reload it when needed
Show the answer

Answer: D. External memory outside the window is the reliable store.

S4Subagents are duplicating each other's searches. What is the most likely cause and fix?

  • AParallel tool calls are enabled; disable them everywhere
  • BThe briefs lack clear objectives and task boundaries; give each subagent a distinct objective and scope
  • CThe lead agent has too many tools; remove the lead's ability to plan
  • DThe model is too small, so every subagent should be replaced with the largest available model and the lead agent removed
Show the answer

Answer: B. Duplicated work means the briefs lack distinct objectives and task boundaries, so each subagent needs a clear scope and output format.

S5A multi-agent system fails midway through a long run. What design supports recovery?

  • ADisabling retries to avoid repeating work that has already been done by earlier steps in the run
  • BRestarting the whole run from the beginning each time a tool call fails or a subagent times out
  • CCheckpointing state so the run resumes from the last good step
  • DIncreasing max_tokens on all agents
Show the answer

Answer: C. Checkpointing state lets a long run resume from the last good step instead of repeating expensive work after a failure.

S6Which TWO are valid reasons to keep subagents' contexts isolated? Select TWO.

  • AIt allows subagents to share every credential
  • BIt guarantees that subagents never make errors
  • CIt removes the need for any briefing or objectives
  • DIt keeps verbose exploration out of the lead's context window
  • EIt lets subagents return short summaries instead of raw transcripts
Show the answer

Answer: D, E. Isolation protects the lead's context and keeps hand-offs compact.

S7How should a release of a long-running agent system be deployed?

  • AGradually shift traffic between versions so agents that are mid-process are not broken
  • BStop all running agents and discard their state
  • CReplace all running instances at once during off-hours, so that no agent is ever mid-process during release
  • DDeploy to every region simultaneously for consistency
Show the answer

Answer: A. Agents are mid-process, so gradual (rainbow) deployments avoid disruption.

S8Which decomposition fits a task where the number of subtasks depends on the input?

  • AA static routing table with one path per document type
  • BA fixed sequence of five prompts defined at design time and executed identically for every input
  • CHierarchical decomposition by an orchestrator at run time
  • DA single prompt with all instructions combined
Show the answer

Answer: C. When the number of subtasks depends on the input, a run-time orchestrator must discover and assign them dynamically.

S9An evaluation of a multi-agent system should begin with which approach?

  • ACounting only the number of tool calls made
  • BA small sample (about 20 queries) scored by an LLM judge with a rubric, plus human testing
  • CA large benchmark run once at the end of development
  • DChecking that every agent follows the same fixed sequence of steps as the reference implementation did
Show the answer

Answer: B. Start small, grade outcomes with a rubric, and add human testing.

S10Token usage of a proposed multi-agent design is about 15 times that of a chat. Which question should the architect ask?

  • ACan the agents be given larger context windows so that the multiple can be reduced to a small number?
  • BIs the value of the result high enough, and parallel enough, to justify that cost?
  • CCan the effort level be raised to make each agent more thorough?
  • DCan the number of agents be doubled to cut wall-clock time further?
Show the answer

Answer: B. The design pays off only when value and parallelism justify the token multiple.

7Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Cost Agents about 4x chat tokens; multi-agent about 15x
Worth it High value, parallelizable, beyond one context window
Poor fit Heavy shared context, many dependencies (most coding)
Lead agent Plan, delegate, synthesize; save plan externally
Subagent brief Objective, format, tool guidance, boundaries
Isolation Own context; return summaries
Decompose Sequence · data partition · role · dependency · hierarchical
Production Checkpoint, trace, rainbow deploy, budgets
Evaluate About 20 queries, LLM judge rubric, human testing
